source.title: NeuroCartography: Scalable Automatic Visual Summarization of Concepts in Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Haekyu Park; Nilaksh Das; Rahul Duggal; Austin P. Wright; Omar Shaikh; Fred Hohman; Duen Horng Chau

record.tranche_reason: The study reports results about how well people recognize and describe groups of neurons, but it does not test any listed version’s claims about individual neuron poles, the cited polysemantic example, cross-model shares, attribution graphs, or explanation scoring on held-out activations.
record.gate_note: The human evaluation measures coherence and interpretability of neuron clusters, not the share of individual neuron poles with one job or whether explanations predict activations on unseen inputs. The classic cat/car example is cited from prior work rather than tested here. The concept-cascade demonstrations are manually initiated and are not tests of the listed versions.
record.test_reason: NeuroCartography is a tool for clustering InceptionV1 neurons, validated by human cluster-inclusion and label-consistency tests. It reports no share of single-job neurons, no cross-model shares, and no reanalysis of the cat/car neuron, which it only cites as polysemantic. It has no tool-quality trend, no neuron-based attribution graphs, and no held-out activation prediction or simulation scoring. Its results bear on cluster coherence, a different construct, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that NeuroCartography scalably finds neuron groups that humans judge to be coherent, meaningful concepts, nearly matching hand-picked clusters. They note the method cannot split polysemantic neurons such as the cat-face/car-front neuron.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops activation-overlap clustering and co-occurrence embeddings for InceptionV1 image neurons and evaluates cluster interpretability with human judgments. It does not use the Qwen neuron-pole audit or language-model explanation-and-scoring procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: not stated for the claim-related human evaluation; the paper reports tuning clustering hyperparameters but does not report that those choices changed these evaluation outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Human raters recognized NeuroCartography InceptionV1 neuron clusters well above chance (FPR 11.8% vs random 30.6%; AUC 0.91 vs hand-picked 0.97). Labels within a cluster were more similar than labels across clusters (0.51 vs 0.301).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Automatically discovered groups of co-activating InceptionV1 neurons are human-interpretable as coherent concepts, nearly as much as hand-picked groups.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
record.problems: The evaluation concerns neuron clusters rather than individual neuron poles or held-out activation prediction. It evaluates one image-classification model, and concepts are manually labeled. The paper also says the method is not designed to dissect polysemantic neurons.

untested.parts: All: no Qwen3-32B or per-neuron audit shares.
All: one vision model only, no language models.
All: the cat/car neuron is cited from Olah et al. as polysemantic but not reanalyzed.
All: no comparison across tools or architectures and no interpretable-share estimates.
All: concept-cascade graphs are qualitative and not evaluated as behaviour explanations.
All: no test of whether explanations predict firing on new inputs.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses classification is correct. All rows evaluate the study's own method and bear on no version. The only claim-adjacent content is the limitation section, which calls the InceptionV1 cat/car neuron polysemantic, citing prior work. That contrasts with V3's reading, but it is a citation, not a result. The curve-detector and watermark-neuron observations are qualitative usage scenarios.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit and all stated shares of one-job, two-related-job, and not-yet-understood neuron poles.
Other language models, dense and mixture-of-experts models, and scaling up to trillions of parameters.

Whether InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron detects a coherent shared pose feature or reflects recursive generalization rather than superposition. The paper cites a prior example of a neuron responding to cat faces, car fronts, and cat legs but does not reanalyze it.

Whether architecture, regularization, or tool quality explains messy neurons; whether interpretability shares rise with better tools or modern architectures; and the stated InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates.
Whether attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons explain behavior without a trained replacement model or its reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fit to activating examples fail to predict firing on other inputs.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.
